units.text: Start with the local rack and the first panel. S3 on Outposts keeps objects on the Outpost for local processing and residency requirements. Local storage still has defined access and operational boundaries.
Move to the access model. Use an S3 on Outposts access point and an Outposts endpoint. Objects use the OUTPOSTS storage class; do not treat this as an ordinary regional bucket.

Inspect the encryption panel. Server-side encryption with S3-managed keys is the default, and customer-provided keys are optional. S3 on Outposts does not support server-side encryption with KMS keys.

Return to the complete slide. Capacity is finite, so monitor free space and verify supported features. Plan supported DataSync transfers deliberately; using S3 APIs does not automatically create regional copies or unlimited storage.
Begin with the subnet-association panel. Use nonoverlapping client and destination address ranges, associate the target subnets and verify access to the local VPC before expanding connectivity.
Move to the peered or on-premises destination panel. Configure destination routes and authorization. The associated subnet also needs a working route through the peer, VPN or Direct Connect path.
Inspect security and return traffic. Permit the application at the destination, check network ACLs and verify the return route. Confirm which source address the destination sees after translation.

With the full slide visible, check internet access and consistency. Internet access needs a default endpoint route, authorization and suitable egress. Give every associated subnet equivalent destination routes and verify DNS to avoid intermittent failures.
Start with the customer-side panel. A customer gateway resource describes your VPN device; it is not the device itself. Select and configure the supported physical or software appliance.
Move to the tunnel endpoints. In the common public-IP design, use the device's static public address, or the NAT device's public address when the appliance is behind NAT.

Inspect IPsec configuration and the firewall reminder. Configure both tunnels with matching IKE, IPsec and authentication settings. Permit required traffic, including UDP 500 and UDP 4500 when NAT traversal is used.

Return to the complete diagram. Configure BGP or supported static routing, AWS subnet routes and the customer return path. Test each tunnel and failure scenario; an UP status does not prove application reachability.

Follow the client-to-gateway diagram and the first panel. Choose VPC subnet associations or native Transit Gateway association for an endpoint. The two association models cannot be mixed on one endpoint.
Move to explicit access. Add destination routes to the Client VPN endpoint and configure network-based authorization. Automatic propagation from Transit Gateway does not supply these endpoint routes.
Inspect the preserved-address panel. Native Transit Gateway integration retains the client source address without source NAT. Destination networks need routes back to the Client VPN address range.

With the full slide restored, check the boundaries. The endpoint and Transit Gateway must share a Region, and address ranges must not overlap. Security-group-based authorization is unsupported for this model; all routing and authorization layers must agree.
